intro: Fifteen verses in two panels that do not obviously belong together: the first six are sky, sun and the silent speech of creation, the next four are the Torah, named six different ways in three verses, and the last four are the speaker, who has said nothing until then. In the Ashkenazi rite it is one of the psalms added to the morning service on Shabbat and festivals, and its closing line is the sentence that ends every Amidah. The thing to watch is verses 8 to 10. The same skeleton runs six times: a noun bound to the divine name, an adjective, then a participle with its object. Learn one and you have learned all six.

stichs.en: For the chief musician. A psalm of David.

verses.summary: The heading. Three words fix the psalm as a piece handed to the temple singers, before a single image arrives.

stichs.en: The heavens are recounting the glory of God,
and the work of His hands the firmament tells.

verses.summary: Creation is given a mouth. Both verbs are participles, continuous: the sky is not reporting an event, it is permanently mid-sentence.

stichs.en: Day to day pours out speech,
and night to night declares knowledge.

verses.summary: The report runs on a shift system, day handing over to day and night to night, which is why it never stops long enough to be checked.

stichs.en: There is no speech,
there are no words,
their voice goes unheard.

verses.summary: The paradox stated flatly: speech with no sound. Whether that means the testimony is silent or that it reaches everywhere is the crux of the first half.

stichs.en: Through all the earth their line goes out,
and to the end of the world their words.
For the sun He set a tent among them,

verses.summary: The soundless message covers the whole earth anyway, and the last three words plant the sun inside it, which is where the psalm gets its second image.

stichs.en: and he is like a bridegroom coming out of his canopy,
he rejoices like a champion to run the course.

verses.summary: The sun gets two comparisons, a bridegroom and a runner, and both are about energy at the start of something rather than endurance through it.

stichs.en: From the end of the heavens is his rising,
and his circuit runs to their ends,
and nothing is hidden from his heat.

verses.summary: The sun's route is total, end to end, with nothing outside its heat. This closes the first panel, and the idea of what can be hidden carries into the second.

stichs.en: The teaching of the LORD is whole, restoring the soul;
the testimony of the LORD is trustworthy, making the simple wise.

verses.summary: The subject changes without warning from sun to Torah. Two clauses, each a noun bound to the divine name, an adjective, then a participle saying what it does to a person.

stichs.en: The precepts of the LORD are upright, gladdening the heart;
the commandment of the LORD is clear, lighting up the eyes.

verses.summary: The same frame twice more. The effects accumulate inward and outward at once: soul, then simple mind, then heart, then eyes.

stichs.en: The fear of the LORD is pure, standing for ever;
the judgments of the LORD are truth, they are righteous altogether.

verses.summary: The sixth and last of the terms, and the only pair that ends in a finite verb rather than a participle: the judgments do not act on you, they simply are right.

stichs.en: They are more desirable than gold, than much fine gold,
and sweeter than honey and the drip of the comb.

verses.summary: The list closes with a price and a taste. Gold is what the teaching is worth, honey is what it is like, and neither is an argument.

stichs.en: Your servant too is warned by them;
in keeping them, great reward.

verses.summary: The speaker enters his own psalm for the first time, and enters it as a servant rather than as an observer of the sky.

stichs.en: Who can discern his own errors?
Clear me of what is hidden.

verses.summary: The turn from praise to petition. Nothing is hidden from the sun's heat, but a person's own faults are hidden from him, and that asymmetry is the problem.

stichs.en: Hold Your servant back also from the insolent;
let them not rule over me.
Then I shall be blameless and clear of great transgression.

verses.summary: The second request, and the harder one: not to be cleared of what he did not see, but to be held back from what he would choose.

stichs.en: May the words of my mouth be acceptable,
and the meditation of my heart, before You,
O LORD, my rock and my redeemer.

verses.summary: The psalm ends by submitting its own words for inspection, applying to the poem the same request it just made about hidden faults.

pardes.body: Two panels and a hinge. Verses 2 to 7 are the sky: heavens, firmament, day, night, then the sun crossing from one end of the world to the other. Verses 8 to 11 are the teaching, named six times in three verses with the same grammatical frame each time. Verses 12 to 15 are the speaker, who has been absent until then. Nothing states what joins the panels, but the vocabulary builds it: {{7.7}} says nothing is hidden from the sun, and six verses later {{13.3}} asks to be cleared of hidden things, the same root both times. The psalm moves from a light nothing escapes to a light that reaches what a person cannot see in himself.

Verse 4 is the known difficulty. Read one way, {{4.4}} makes the line say there is no speech and no words and their voice is unheard, so creation testifies in silence. Read the other way it says there are no words whose sound is not heard, so the testimony reaches everyone, and translators still split over it. Verse 5 has a second crux: {{5.3}} is the ordinary word for a measuring line or cord, which sits awkwardly in parallel with words in the next clause, and the ancient Greek version renders it as their sound, which points to a different reading of the consonants. The sun's tent in verse 6 is {{6.3}}, the noun that later Hebrew uses for a wedding canopy, which is why a bridegroom follows it so naturally.

The six terms of verses 8 to 10 are the compact source of a much longer list: Psalm 119 runs the same vocabulary of teaching, testimony, precepts, commandment and judgments across all twenty-two of its acrostic sections. Verse 13 has left the clearer mark on practice. Asking to be cleared of faults one cannot discern is the logic behind confessing sins known and unknown, and the psalm keeps the two categories apart: {{13.3}} is what a person cannot see and asks to be purged of, while verse 14 is what he can see and asks to be restrained from. One is cleansing, the other is protection, and the psalm does not treat them as the same request.

In the kabbalistic reading the six terms are stages rather than synonyms, one teaching received at six depths, each named for the faculty it reaches: soul, then untrained mind, then heart, then eyes. The sun in its canopy carries the standard image for light that has to be housed before it can be given, since bare light burns rather than illuminates, and note that the tent of verse 5 is set among them, inside the created order rather than above it. The last verse offers speech and the unspoken movement of the heart in one breath, {{15.0}} governing both, which is read as the moment a person hands back his outer and inner levels together.
